lesson.title: Which Way Will the Water Go? Predicting Movement with Water Potential
lesson.summary: Water potential is a single number that combines solute concentration and physical pressure to predict exactly which direction water will move across a membrane.
lesson.body:
Osmosis tells you that water moves toward the side with more dissolved solute, but that simple rule breaks down as soon as physical pressure enters the picture, and in real cells it almost always does. Water potential, abbreviated with the Greek letter psi, solves this problem by folding both effects into one measurable quantity, expressed in units of pressure such as megapascals. Pure water at atmospheric pressure is defined as zero, and every other situation is described relative to that baseline. The rule that governs everything else in this chapter is simple: water always moves from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential, the same way heat flows from hot to cold.

Water potential has two main components that add together, solute potential and pressure potential. Solute potential, sometimes called osmotic potential, reflects the concentration of dissolved particles. Because dissolved solutes tie up water molecules through hydrogen bonding, the polar water molecules cluster around ions and polar solutes instead of moving freely, which lowers the water's capacity to do work. Solute potential is therefore always zero or negative, and it becomes more negative as solute concentration rises. This is the same hydrogen bonding behavior that makes water such an effective solvent in the first place, so the polarity of water is the reason solute potential exists at all.

Pressure potential is the physical push exerted on water, and unlike solute potential it can be positive, negative, or zero. In a plant cell, the rigid cell wall resists the inward pressure created as water enters, and that resistance generates a positive pressure potential. In the xylem of a tall tree, by contrast, the pull of transpiration creates tension, a negative pressure potential that helps draw water upward. Adding solute potential and pressure potential together gives total water potential, and this sum is what actually determines which way water moves, not solute concentration alone.

Consider two plant cells connected by a thin layer of extracellular fluid. One cell has just taken up a large amount of sugar, lowering its solute potential well below that of its neighbor. If both cells otherwise have similar pressure potential, water will move by osmosis into the sugar-loaded cell, following its own gradient, from high water potential to low water potential. Now suppose that same cell has already swollen and its wall is pushing back hard, raising its pressure potential enough to offset the low solute potential. Its total water potential could equal that of its neighbor, and net water movement would stop entirely. That equilibrium point is exactly the situation covered next, where the buildup of pressure potential inside a walled cell is what produces turgor.

Animal cells complicate the story in an instructive way, because they lack a rigid wall and therefore cannot build up a meaningful pressure potential. For a red blood cell sitting in blood plasma, water potential is governed almost entirely by solute potential, which is why placing red blood cells in distilled water causes them to swell and eventually burst, while placing them in a concentrated salt solution causes them to shrivel. Plant cells survive the equivalent hypotonic situation because the wall supplies the missing pressure term. Water potential is ultimately a bookkeeping tool, but it is the tool that lets biologists predict, quantitatively, exactly how water will move through soil, roots, stems, leaves, and every membrane in between.
